title: Genomic Medicine and Precision Therapeutics
answer: Polygenic risk, gene editing design, pharmacogenomics, epigenetic age and rare disease diagnosis.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Polygenic Risk Scores
children.blurb: Polygenic risk scores are numbers that summarise the combined effect of many small genetic variants on the chance of developing a condition such as coronary artery disease, type 2 diabetes or breast cancer.

children.name: Gene Editing Guide Design
children.blurb: Gene editing guide design is the work of choosing the RNA sequence and delivery format that will direct an editing tool to one intended site in a genome and few others.

children.name: Pharmacogenomics
children.blurb: Pharmacogenomics is the study of how inherited genetic variation changes a person's response to a drug, covering both how the body processes a medicine and how the medicine acts on its target.

children.name: Epigenetic Aging Clocks
children.blurb: Epigenetic aging clocks are models that estimate biological age from DNA methylation patterns measured across selected sites in the genome.

children.name: Rare Disease Diagnosis
children.blurb: Rare disease diagnosis covers the use of computational methods to identify conditions that individually affect few people but collectively are common, often after a long diagnostic odyssey.

sections.body: Genomic medicine applies artificial intelligence to the readout of a person's DNA and the molecules that regulate it. Polygenic risk scores combine thousands of small genetic variants into a single number that estimates susceptibility to conditions such as heart disease or type 2 diabetes. Gene editing guide design uses models to propose the short RNA sequences that steer enzymes like CRISPR to the right spot in the genome and to predict which off target cuts are likely. Pharmacogenomics matches variants in drug metabolizing genes to how a patient processes specific medicines. Epigenetic aging clocks estimate biological age from chemical marks on DNA, and rare disease diagnosis tools search a patient's exome or genome against databases of known pathogenic variants. All of this is running now in research pipelines and, in some cases, clinical laboratories.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Polygenic scores are well validated for a handful of common conditions in populations of European ancestry and degrade in accuracy for others, which is a known and unresolved fairness problem. Guide design has become reliable enough that most editing experiments start with a model's ranked candidates, but predicting unintended edits across the whole genome remains imperfect. Pharmacogenomic guidance exists for a limited set of gene drug pairs, and many hospitals still lack the infrastructure to return results at the point of prescribing. Epigenetic clocks correlate with age and mortality risk in cohorts, yet no clock has been shown to be a target that changes outcomes when altered. Rare disease diagnosis is the strongest success story, with sequencing plus AI interpretation ending diagnostic odysseys for some families, though roughly half of cases still go unsolved. The honest limits are reference panel bias, sparse functional evidence for most variants, and the gap between a statistical association and a clinical decision.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here form a chain from population risk to individual mechanism. Polygenic Risk Scores is the entry point for inherited susceptibility and the statistical machinery behind it. Rare Disease Diagnosis sits at the opposite end, where a single high impact variant rather than a thousand small ones explains a patient's illness. Gene Editing Guide Design covers the therapeutic intervention side, the computational work that precedes any attempt to correct a sequence. Pharmacogenomics handles the everyday question of which drug and dose suit a given genotype, and Epigenetic Aging Clocks addresses the regulatory layer that sits above the sequence and changes with age and environment. A reader interested in prevention should start with polygenic scores, one chasing a diagnosis should start with rare disease, and one thinking about treatment should move between editing design and pharmacogenomics.
